title: Links in text must not rely on color alone
summary: A link inside a paragraph is told apart from the text only by its color. Add an underline, or another visible cue, so it stands out.
problem: A link within a block of text has no underline, bold or other visual cue, and its color is too close to the surrounding text color. The link color here, #1a56a8, differs from the body color #333333 by a contrast ratio below 3 to 1, so the difference is easy to miss.
whoItAffects: People with color vision deficiency, who may see the link and the text as the same color, and people with low vision. Anyone reading on a washed-out screen can also miss links that only differ in hue.
whyItMatters: A link nobody notices is never followed, so key information and next steps are missed. This is a WCAG 1.4.1 failure at Level A, the baseline that accessibility regulations and procurement requirements commonly build on.
steps: Find the links inside paragraphs, lists and other text in the scan result.
Add text-decoration: underline to those links. This is the clearest cue and the one people expect.
If you remove underlines for design reasons, give the link a 3 to 1 contrast ratio against the surrounding text, and add another cue such as bold or an underline on hover and focus.
Keep the link color at 4.5 to 1 against the background so it stays readable.

howToCheck: Look at the page in grayscale, or with a color blindness simulator in your browser's developer tools. If you cannot spot the links inside the paragraphs, they rely on color alone.
